bacterial_growth_modeling.description: Mathematical modeling of bacterial population growth using logistic, Monod, Gompertz, and Baranyi models to predict lag phase, exponential growth, and stationary phase dynamics.

growth_rate_mu.description: Maximum specific growth rate (h^-1), often expressed as doubling time (td = ln2/mu).

e_coli_LB_37C.when: E. coli K-12 or B strains in LB broth at 37C with aeration
e_coli_LB_37C.why: Rich medium provides all amino acids and vitamins; optimal temperature for E. coli

e_coli_M9_minimal_37C.when: E. coli in M9 minimal + glucose at 37C
e_coli_M9_minimal_37C.why: Cells must synthesize all amino acids and cofactors de novo; slower growth

b_subtilis_LB_37C.why: Gram-positive; slightly slower than E. coli under equivalent conditions

s_aureus_37C.when: S. aureus in rich media at 37C

p_aeruginosa_37C.value_or_range: mu ~ 0.6-0.9 h^-1 (doubling time ~45-70 min in vitro)
p_aeruginosa_37C.when: P. aeruginosa in standard lab media at 37C
p_aeruginosa_37C.why: Versatile metabolism but somewhat slower; in chronic lung infections doubling time can be 100-200 min

m_tuberculosis.when: M. tuberculosis in Middlebrook 7H9 or Lowenstein-Jensen media
m_tuberculosis.why: Extremely slow grower due to complex cell wall biosynthesis; mycolic acid synthesis rate-limiting

common_mistakes: Using LB growth rates for minimal media simulations (3-fold error)
Assuming constant growth rate across all growth phases
Ignoring strain-specific differences (lab strains vs clinical isolates)
Not accounting for aeration — anaerobic growth of E. coli is 2-3x slower

carrying_capacity_K.description: Maximum population density achievable in a given medium, limited by nutrient depletion or waste accumulation.

LB_broth.when: Overnight E. coli culture in LB at 37C with shaking
LB_broth.why: Limited by carbon source availability; LB is amino acid-rich but carbon-poor

M9_glucose_minimal.value_or_range: 1e8 to 5e9 CFU/mL (OD600 ~ 0.5-2 depending on glucose conc)
M9_glucose_minimal.why: Carbon-limited; carrying capacity scales with initial glucose concentration

rich_defined_media.why: Higher nutrient content than LB; often used for protein expression

common_mistakes: Assuming OD600 linearly correlates with CFU/mL above OD 0.4
Not considering that stationary phase cells lose viability over time
Using carrying capacity from one medium in simulations for another medium

temperature_dependence.description: Growth rate dependence on temperature, typically described by Q10 or Arrhenius models.

mesophile_Q10.why: Enzymatic reaction rates roughly double per 10C increase within optimal range

arrhenius_model.when: Limited temperature range modeling (not near extremes)
arrhenius_model.why: Arrhenius model breaks down near Tmin and Tmax; only valid in middle range

beyond_optimum.value_or_range: Growth rate drops sharply above Topt (use Cardinal Temperature Model)
beyond_optimum.when: Temperatures approaching Tmax for the organism
beyond_optimum.why: Protein denaturation and membrane disruption dominate; Arrhenius invalid here

common_mistakes: Extrapolating Arrhenius model beyond the linear range of the ln(mu) vs 1/T plot
Assuming Q10 is constant across the entire growth temperature range
Ignoring cold shock and heat shock responses that transiently alter growth

model_selection.description: Choosing between logistic, Gompertz, Baranyi, and other growth models.

use_baranyi.value_or_range: Baranyi-Roberts model (4 parameters: mu, K, lag, initial pop)
use_baranyi.when: When lag phase is important and you need mechanistic lag representation; predictive food microbiology
use_baranyi.why: Baranyi model gives least error in cell number and has mechanistic basis for lag (Q0 parameter represents physiological state); superior to Gompertz for most datasets

use_gompertz.when: Quick empirical fits where model simplicity is valued; historical comparisons
use_gompertz.why: Most widely used historically but tends to overestimate maximum population density; Baranyi and Richards models shown to be significantly superior

use_logistic.value_or_range: Logistic model (3 parameters: r, K, N0)
use_logistic.when: Simple symmetric growth without explicit lag phase; theoretical ecology models
use_logistic.why: Assumes symmetric growth curve (inflection at K/2), which is often not biologically realistic; no lag phase

use_monod.when: Continuous culture (chemostat); substrate-limited growth; wastewater modeling
use_monod.why: Explicitly links growth to substrate concentration; steady-state continuous culture

common_mistakes: Using batch culture parameters (logistic K) for continuous culture (chemostat) simulations
Using Gompertz when Baranyi gives significantly better fits for the same data
Applying Monod kinetics to batch culture without accounting for changing substrate concentration
Ignoring death phase — none of these standard models capture it well

monod_Ks.description: Half-saturation constant in Monod kinetics — substrate concentration at which growth rate is half of mu_max.

glucose_aerobic.value_or_range: Ks = 2-10 mg/L for E. coli (some report up to 50 mg/L depending on strain)
glucose_aerobic.when: Aerobic growth on glucose as sole carbon source
glucose_aerobic.why: E. coli has high-affinity glucose transporters (PTS system); Ks is relatively low

wastewater_heterogeneous.value_or_range: Ks = 25-100 mg COD/L for mixed cultures
wastewater_heterogeneous.why: Mixed substrates and mixed cultures give higher apparent Ks

common_mistakes: Treating Ks as a fixed constant — it varies with temperature, pH, and microbial community
Using pure-culture Ks values for mixed-culture wastewater models
Confusing Ks (growth) with Km (enzyme kinetics) — different concepts even if mathematically similar

bacterial_growth_modeling.best_practice_notes: Always report growth conditions (medium, temperature, aeration, pH) alongside growth parameters. Use Baranyi model for food safety applications. Validate model fits with RMSE and AIC/BIC model comparison. For simulations, use species-specific and condition-specific parameters from BioNumbers or primary literature rather than textbook defaults.

lotka_volterra_community_dynamics.description: Generalized Lotka-Volterra (gLV) models for simulating microbial community dynamics, predicting species coexistence, and analyzing interaction networks.

interaction_coefficients_aij.description: Pairwise interaction strength between species i and j. Positive = mutualism/commensalism, negative = competition/amensalism.

gut_microbiome.value_or_range: Typically |aij| in range 0.01-1.0 (normalized); most interactions are weak (|aij| < 0.1)
gut_microbiome.when: Modeling gut microbial communities from 16S time-series data
gut_microbiome.why: Strong interactions are rare in stable ecosystems; weak interactions dominate and promote stability

synthetic_community.value_or_range: |aij| can be 0.1-5.0 for defined consortia of 2-15 species
synthetic_community.when: In vitro defined communities with known metabolic interactions
synthetic_community.why: Controlled conditions allow stronger measurable interactions; metabolic cross-feeding dominates

nasal_community.value_or_range: Model validity depends on environmental complexity and nutrient conditions
nasal_community.when: gLV works well in complex (many mediators), low-nutrient environments
nasal_community.why: gLV accuracy declines with high metabolite leakage and niche overlap; simple environments break the gLV assumption

common_mistakes: Inferring interaction coefficients from relative abundance data without converting to absolute abundances
Assuming symmetric interactions (aij = aji) — most microbial interactions are asymmetric
Ignoring higher-order interactions which can stabilize or destabilize communities
Overfitting gLV to sparse time-series data with too many species

growth_rate_ri.description: Intrinsic growth rate of species i in the absence of other species.

from_monoculture.value_or_range: Estimated from monoculture growth curves; typically 0.1-2.0 h^-1
from_monoculture.when: Each species cultured individually under the same conditions
from_monoculture.why: Monoculture growth rate is the baseline for gLV; assumes no inter-species effects

common_mistakes: Using literature growth rates from different media/conditions than the community experiment

number_of_species.description: Number of species to include in the gLV model.

practical_limit.value_or_range: 2-20 species for parameter-identifiable models; >20 requires regularization
practical_limit.when: Fitting gLV parameters from time-series data
practical_limit.why: N species requires N^2 interaction parameters; identifiability becomes impossible with sparse data for large N

compositional_approach.value_or_range: Use compositional Lotka-Volterra (cLV) for relative abundance data from sequencing
compositional_approach.when: Only relative abundance data available (16S, metagenomics) without absolute quantification
compositional_approach.why: Standard gLV requires absolute abundances; cLV unifies gLV with compositional data analysis

common_mistakes: Simulating 100+ species without adequate time-series data for parameter estimation
Using gLV for strongly resource-coupled systems where consumer-resource models are more appropriate
Not checking structural identifiability before fitting

stability_analysis.description: Eigenvalue analysis of the interaction matrix to predict community stability.

may_wigner.value_or_range: Community unstable when sigma * sqrt(N * C) > 1 (May's stability criterion)
may_wigner.when: Random interaction matrices; large diverse communities
may_wigner.why: sigma = interaction strength std dev, N = species count, C = connectance; predicts diversity-stability relationship

common_mistakes: Concluding instability from eigenvalue analysis without checking if the steady state is ecologically feasible (all abundances positive)
Ignoring that real communities may persist in non-equilibrium states

lotka_volterra_community_dynamics.best_practice_notes: Start with small defined communities (2-6 species) for parameter estimation before scaling up. Use time-resolved absolute abundance data when possible. Consider compositional Lotka-Volterra (cLV) for sequencing data. Always perform stability analysis and check for feasibility of steady states. Validate predictions with hold-out experiments (e.g., train on pairs, predict triplets).

anaerobic_digestion_adm1.description: Anaerobic Digestion Model No. 1 (ADM1) by IWA for simulating biogas production from organic waste. Includes 26 dynamic state variables and models disintegration, hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis.

hydraulic_retention_time_HRT.description: Average time liquid remains in the digester (days).

food_waste_mesophilic.when: Single-stage mesophilic (35-37C) digestion of source-separated food waste
food_waste_mesophilic.why: Shorter HRT risks VFA accumulation and washout of slow-growing methanogens; longer HRT reduces throughput

sewage_sludge_mesophilic.why: Sludge is less readily degradable than food waste; longer HRT needed for hydrolysis

manure_mesophilic.value_or_range: 15-30 days (cow manure), up to 60 days for poultry manure
manure_mesophilic.why: Lignocellulosic content requires longer hydrolysis; poultry manure has high ammonia inhibition risk

thermophilic.why: Faster hydrolysis and methanogenesis at higher temperature; but higher instability risk

common_mistakes: Setting HRT too short causes washout of methanogens (SRT must exceed methanogen doubling time of ~10-12 days)
Not distinguishing between HRT (liquid) and SRT (solids) in systems with recirculation

organic_loading_rate_OLR.description: Rate of organic matter fed to the digester, typically in kg VS/(m^3*day).

food_waste_stable.why: Food waste is rapidly hydrolyzable; OLR >5 causes VFA accumulation and pH crash

food_waste_thermophilic_optimum.value_or_range: 2.5 g VS/L/day optimal (yields ~541 mL CH4/g VS)
food_waste_thermophilic_optimum.why: Higher microbial activity but also higher VFA production; narrow stable window

food_waste_mesophilic_optimum.value_or_range: 1.5 g VS/L/day optimal (yields ~371 mL CH4/g VS)
food_waste_mesophilic_optimum.why: Lower optimal OLR but more stable operation

two_stage_system.value_or_range: Can handle up to 6-10 kg VS/m^3/day with phase separation
two_stage_system.why: pH optimization in each stage prevents inhibition; acidogenic stage tolerates higher OLR

common_mistakes: Increasing OLR too rapidly without monitoring VFA/alkalinity ratio
Not accounting for OLR spikes from variable feedstock composition

VFA_threshold.description: Total volatile fatty acid concentration as process stability indicator.

healthy_operation.value_or_range: Total VFA < 1500 mg/L (as acetic acid equivalent); VFA/alkalinity ratio < 0.3
healthy_operation.why: Balanced acidogenesis and methanogenesis; methanogens consuming VFA as fast as produced

early_warning.value_or_range: Total VFA 1500-4000 mg/L; VFA/alkalinity > 0.3-0.5; propionic/acetic acid ratio > 1.4
early_warning.why: Propionic acid accumulation is especially indicative of stress — thermodynamically unfavorable degradation

process_failure.why: Below pH 6.5, undissociated VFAs become toxic to methanogens; positive feedback loop

common_mistakes: Monitoring only total VFA without speciation (propionic acid is more problematic than acetic)
Relying on pH alone — alkalinity can buffer pH while VFA accumulates dangerously

temperature_regime.description: Operating temperature selection between mesophilic and thermophilic.

mesophilic.when: Standard operation; priority is process stability; moderate feedstock
mesophilic.why: More stable operation, lower energy input, more diverse microbial community provides buffering

thermophilic.when: High-throughput processing; pathogen destruction needed; readily degradable substrate
thermophilic.why: Higher methane production rate (up to 50% increase), better pathogen kill, shorter HRT needed; but higher ammonia inhibition from free NH3

temperature_phased.why: 50.3% higher methane yield than single mesophilic; 32.7% higher than single thermophilic

common_mistakes: Switching between mesophilic and thermophilic without proper transition period (>3 SRT needed)
Not accounting for increased free ammonia at higher temperatures (pKa shift)

methane_yield.description: Specific methane production per unit of volatile solids added.

food_waste.value_or_range: 370-540 mL CH4/g VS (BMP; theoretical max ~530 mL CH4/g VS)
food_waste.why: High lipid and protein content gives high methane potential

sewage_sludge.when: Mixed primary and secondary sewage sludge
sewage_sludge.why: Variable composition; secondary sludge is more recalcitrant

common_mistakes: Reporting methane yield without specifying STP conditions (0C, 1 atm) vs actual temperature
Confusing VS-added basis with VS-destroyed basis
Not accounting for methane dissolved in digestate (2-5% at mesophilic conditions)

anaerobic_digestion_adm1.best_practice_notes: Always perform biochemical methane potential (BMP) tests before continuous digestion. Monitor VFA speciation (not just total), alkalinity, pH, and biogas composition simultaneously. ADM1 has 26 state variables — calibrate hydrolysis rate constant (khyd) and inhibition constants for each new substrate. Use ADM1F (open-source) for accessible implementation. Ensure correct fractionation of substrate into carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids for ADM1 input.

flux_balance_analysis.description: Constraint-based metabolic modeling using FBA, pFBA, and FVA to predict metabolic flux distributions in genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs).

objective_function.description: The cellular objective to maximize or minimize in the linear program.

biomass_maximization.when: Predicting growth rate, essential genes, growth phenotypes; exponential growth phase
biomass_maximization.why: Cells under selection pressure (evolution) tend to maximize growth; validated for E. coli, S. cerevisiae

ATP_maintenance.when: Stationary phase, stress conditions, non-growing cells
ATP_maintenance.why: Non-growing cells optimize energy for maintenance rather than biomass

product_maximization.when: Metabolic engineering; predicting theoretical maximum yield
product_maximization.why: Useful for strain design but does not reflect natural cellular objective

common_mistakes: Always using biomass maximization — inappropriate for stationary phase or stress conditions
Not validating objective function choice against experimental flux data (13C-MFA)
Ignoring that the optimal solution is often non-unique (use FVA to assess)

glucose_uptake_constraint.description: Maximum glucose uptake rate, set as lower bound of glucose exchange reaction (negative = import).

e_coli_aerobic_standard.when: Aerobic growth of E. coli on glucose minimal medium
e_coli_aerobic_standard.why: Experimental values range 8-12 mmol/gDW/hr for wild-type; 18.5 is a commonly used upper bound in COBRApy tutorials

e_coli_anaerobic.when: Anaerobic growth (higher glycolytic flux needed for ATP)
e_coli_anaerobic.why: Without oxidative phosphorylation, cells increase glycolytic throughput

common_mistakes: Using wrong units (mmol/gDW/hr vs mmol/L/hr — must be biomass-normalized)
Setting uptake rate too high, creating unrealistic growth predictions
Forgetting the sign convention: negative lower bound = uptake in COBRApy

method_selection.description: Choosing between FBA, pFBA, and FVA for different analysis goals.

use_FBA.when: Quick growth rate prediction; essential gene analysis; simple phenotype prediction
use_FBA.why: Fastest; single LP solve; sufficient for many applications

use_pFBA.value_or_range: Parsimonious FBA (minimize total flux at optimal objective)
use_pFBA.when: Need unique flux distribution; comparing with experimental fluxes; enzyme cost analysis
use_pFBA.why: Eliminates thermodynamically infeasible loops; assumes cells minimize total enzyme investment; more biologically realistic

use_FVA.value_or_range: Flux Variability Analysis (find min/max for each reaction at optimal objective)
use_FVA.when: Assessing solution space; identifying reactions with fixed vs flexible fluxes; robustness analysis
use_FVA.why: Reveals which reactions are tightly constrained vs free to vary; essential for understanding metabolic flexibility

common_mistakes: Interpreting a single FBA solution as THE flux distribution — there may be many equally optimal solutions
Not checking for thermodynamically infeasible loops in FBA solutions (use loopless FBA or pFBA)
Using FVA without setting a fraction of optimum (e.g., require 90% of max biomass)

essential_gene_prediction.description: Using FBA to predict gene essentiality by simulating single-gene knockouts.

validation_rates.value_or_range: ~80-90% accuracy for E. coli (iML1515 model) on glucose minimal; lower on rich media
validation_rates.when: Comparing FBA predictions with experimental knockout libraries (e.g., Keio collection)
validation_rates.why: Rich media allow bypass of many biosynthetic pathways, reducing essentiality; model accuracy depends on medium composition

common_mistakes: Simulating knockouts in rich media without constraining all nutrient uptake reactions
Not accounting for gene-protein-reaction (GPR) associations correctly

flux_balance_analysis.best_practice_notes: Always use the most recent genome-scale model for your organism (e.g., iML1515 for E. coli, Yeast8 for S. cerevisiae). Set exchange reaction bounds to match experimental media conditions. Use pFBA for flux predictions that will be compared with experimental data. Run FVA to understand solution space before interpreting any single FBA solution. Validate predictions against at least growth rate and a few key fluxes measured by 13C-MFA.

michaelis_menten_kinetics.description: Enzyme kinetics modeling using the Michaelis-Menten equation (v = Vmax*[S]/(Km+[S])) to characterize enzyme-substrate interactions, determine kinetic constants, and predict reaction rates.

Km.description: Michaelis constant — substrate concentration at which reaction rate is half of Vmax. Reflects enzyme-substrate affinity (lower Km = higher affinity).

hexokinase_glucose.value_or_range: Km = 0.02-0.13 mM (hexokinase A-C); Km = 5-50 mM (glucokinase/hexokinase D)
hexokinase_glucose.why: Brain hexokinase has low Km to function at low glucose; liver glucokinase has high Km to act as glucose sensor

lactate_dehydrogenase.value_or_range: Km = 0.05-1.0 mM for pyruvate (varies by isoform); Km = 2-18 mM for lactate
lactate_dehydrogenase.why: Different tissue isoforms (H4 vs M4) have different kinetic properties optimized for their metabolic role

catalase_H2O2.why: Very high Km because catalase operates at high substrate concentrations; extremely high kcat (~10^7 s^-1) compensates

CYP_enzymes.value_or_range: Km typically 1-100 uM for drug substrates; highly substrate-dependent
CYP_enzymes.why: CYP enzymes exhibit broad substrate specificity with variable affinities; CYP3A4 often shows atypical kinetics

common_mistakes: Using Km values from one organism/isoform for a different organism without checking BRENDA
Not considering that Km measured in vitro may differ from apparent Km in vivo due to competing substrates
Reporting Km without specifying pH, temperature, and buffer conditions

substrate_concentration_range.description: Range of substrate concentrations needed for reliable Km/Vmax estimation.

standard_fitting.when: Determining Km and Vmax from initial rate measurements
standard_fitting.why: Need data points both well below and well above Km; below Km = first-order region, above Km = saturation region; both are needed for reliable curve fitting

optimal_design.value_or_range: 8-12 substrate concentrations with half near Km and half at high [S]
optimal_design.when: Maximizing information content of experiment (D-optimal design)
optimal_design.why: Fisher information matrix analysis shows measurements near Km and at high [S] are most informative

common_mistakes: Using only 3-4 substrate concentrations — need at least 7-8 for reliable nonlinear regression
All substrate concentrations above Km (cannot resolve Km from apparent zero-order kinetics)
Using Lineweaver-Burk (double reciprocal) plots for parameter estimation — nonlinear regression is statistically superior

when_MM_fails.description: Conditions under which the Michaelis-Menten model is inappropriate.

substrate_inhibition.value_or_range: Use substrate inhibition equation: v = Vmax*[S]/(Km + [S]*(1+[S]/Ki))
substrate_inhibition.when: Velocity decreases at high substrate concentrations; ~20% of enzymes exhibit this
substrate_inhibition.why: Second substrate molecule binds unproductively to ES complex; common in CYP enzymes and many oxidoreductases

cooperativity.when: Sigmoidal v vs [S] curve; multi-subunit enzymes with allosteric regulation
cooperativity.why: Multiple active sites with cooperative binding; does not follow hyperbolic saturation

non_steady_state.value_or_range: Use progress curve analysis or pre-steady-state kinetics
non_steady_state.when: Enzyme concentration comparable to substrate; very fast reactions; single-turnover conditions
non_steady_state.why: Michaelis-Menten assumes [ES] is at steady state — fails when [E]~[S] (typical in vivo)

common_mistakes: Fitting Michaelis-Menten to progress curves (absorbance vs time) instead of initial rates
Ignoring product inhibition in reversible reactions
Not verifying that initial rate conditions are met (< 10% substrate consumed)

michaelis_menten_kinetics.best_practice_notes: Always use BRENDA (brenda-enzymes.org) as the primary source for published Km/Vmax/kcat values. Use nonlinear regression (not Lineweaver-Burk) for parameter fitting. Measure initial rates at 8+ substrate concentrations spanning 0.1*Km to 20*Km. Always check for substrate inhibition by including high [S] points. Report buffer, pH, temperature, and ionic strength with all kinetic constants. Consider using kcat/Km (catalytic efficiency) for comparing enzymes rather than Km alone.

hill_function_dose_response.description: Hill equation modeling for cooperative binding, dose-response curves, and transcriptional regulation: f([L]) = [L]^n / (K_d^n + [L]^n).

hill_coefficient_n.description: Quantifies cooperativity of ligand binding. n=1 = no cooperativity (Michaelis-Menten), n>1 = positive cooperativity, n<1 = negative cooperativity.

hemoglobin_O2.when: O2 binding to hemoglobin (4 subunits, 4 binding sites)
hemoglobin_O2.why: Classic example of positive cooperativity; conformational change in one subunit facilitates binding in adjacent subunits. Note: n < actual binding sites (4) because cooperativity is not infinite

transcription_factor_binding.value_or_range: n = 1.5-4.0 (depends on TF and promoter architecture)
transcription_factor_binding.when: Modeling gene regulation by cooperative TF binding
transcription_factor_binding.why: Adjacent binding sites on DNA allow cooperative binding through protein-protein interactions

drug_dose_response.why: n reflects steepness of response curve; n=1 is standard (no cooperativity), n>1 = steep (switch-like), n<1 = gradual

no_cooperativity.why: Reduces to standard Michaelis-Menten/Langmuir binding; hyperbolic response

common_mistakes: Interpreting Hill coefficient as the number of binding sites — it is an interaction coefficient, typically less than actual binding sites
Using Hill equation for biphasic dose-response curves (two inflection points) — need biphasic model instead
Fitting Hill equation to data that only covers one side of K_d (need data spanning below and above K_d)
Applying Hill equation to systems with negative cooperativity — fits are unreliable for n < 1

K_half.description: Half-maximal effective concentration (EC50/K_d) — ligand concentration at which response is 50%.

pharmacology.value_or_range: Drug-specific; typically nM-uM range for receptor-binding drugs
pharmacology.why: Primary measure of drug potency; lower EC50 = more potent

common_mistakes: Confusing EC50 (functional) with Kd (binding) — they differ when there is receptor reserve
Reporting EC50 without Hill coefficient — steepness matters for dosing

hill_function_dose_response.best_practice_notes: Use at least 10-12 data points spanning 2 log units below and above K_half for reliable Hill fits. Report both K_half and n with confidence intervals. For biphasic responses, use a two-component model rather than forcing a single Hill fit. The Hill equation is a phenomenological model — for mechanistic understanding, use the Adair-Klotz equation or MWC/KNF models.

gene_circuit_design.description: Design and parameterization of synthetic genetic circuits including toggle switches (bistability) and repressilators (oscillations), using mathematical models based on Hill functions and ODEs.

hill_coefficients_repressors.description: Effective Hill coefficient for transcriptional repression, reflecting cooperativity of repressor binding.

LacI_repressor.value_or_range: n = 2-3 (effective; LacI forms tetramers with two operator-binding domains)
LacI_repressor.when: Lac operon regulation; toggle switch circuits using PLlac promoter
LacI_repressor.why: LacI binds as tetramer with cooperative DNA looping between O1 and O3; effective cooperativity depends on operator configuration

TetR_repressor.why: TetR binds as homodimer; cooperativity from multiple operator sites or promoter architecture

CI_lambda_repressor.when: Lambda phage genetic switch; CI/Cro decision circuit
CI_lambda_repressor.why: CI dimers cooperatively bind adjacent operator sites OR1-OR2; long-range cooperativity through DNA looping to OL

common_mistakes: Using n=1 in toggle switch models — bistability requires n > 1 for at least one repressor
Assuming measured Hill coefficient is exactly the number of binding sites
Not accounting for promoter context — same repressor in different promoter configurations gives different effective n

bistability_requirements.description: Conditions for a toggle switch to exhibit bistable behavior (two stable steady states).

minimum_cooperativity.value_or_range: At least one repressor must have Hill coefficient n > 1; both n > 2 gives robust bistability
minimum_cooperativity.why: Gardner et al. (2000) showed bistability requires sufficient nonlinearity; n=1 gives only one stable state. Higher cooperativity widens the bistable parameter region.

balanced_promoters.value_or_range: Promoter strengths (alpha1, alpha2) must be roughly balanced — within 2-5 fold of each other
balanced_promoters.when: Designing toggle switches with two different repressor-promoter pairs
balanced_promoters.why: If one promoter is much stronger, the system is monostable in one state; balance ensures both states are accessible

common_mistakes: Not checking if both steady states are stable (need Jacobian eigenvalue analysis)
Ignoring leaky expression — high basal expression can destroy bistability
Using identical repressor-promoter pairs, making both states equivalent (no useful switching)

repressilator_parameters.description: Parameters controlling oscillation dynamics in the repressilator (three-node negative feedback ring).

oscillation_period.value_or_range: ~150 min (original Elowitz design); 2.4-5.7 cell generations (improved designs)
oscillation_period.when: E. coli expressing lacI-tetR-cI ring with ssrA-tagged proteins
oscillation_period.why: Period determined primarily by protein half-life and repressor strength; removing ssrA tags extends period

minimum_cooperativity_for_oscillation.value_or_range: Hill coefficient n > 1 required; n >= 2 for robust oscillations
minimum_cooperativity_for_oscillation.why: At n=1, system has only one stable fixed point (no oscillations); ultrasensitivity is required for limit cycle oscillations

protein_degradation_rate.value_or_range: With ssrA tag: half-life ~40-60 min; without tag: half-life several hours in E. coli
protein_degradation_rate.why: Comparable mRNA and protein decay rates favor oscillations; ssrA tag increases degradation via ClpXP protease

common_mistakes: Not including protein degradation tags — native E. coli proteins are too stable for fast oscillations
Ignoring growth rate dilution — cell division contributes to effective protein degradation
Designing with too much leakiness — prevents repressilator from achieving low expression states needed for cycling

gene_circuit_design.best_practice_notes: For toggle switches, verify bistability mathematically before building (nullcline analysis). For repressilators, use matched promoter-RBS strengths and include ssrA degradation tags. Test circuits with fluorescent reporters. Consider growth rate coupling — faster growth dilutes proteins faster, affecting circuit dynamics. Use the BioModels database (BIOMD0000000507, BIOMD0000000012) for validated mathematical models.

codon_optimization.description: Optimization of DNA coding sequences for heterologous expression by matching codon usage to host tRNA pools, while considering mRNA structure, codon pair bias, and other factors.

codon_adaptation_index_CAI.description: CAI measures how well codons match the host's preferred codon usage (0 to 1, higher = better adapted).

good_expression_e_coli.when: Heterologous protein expression in E. coli
good_expression_e_coli.why: Highest CAI among all E. coli genes is 0.85 (lpp); CAI > 0.8 indicates codon usage similar to highly expressed native genes; CAI correlates moderately with expression (r ~ 0.5-0.6)

highly_expressed_native.value_or_range: CAI = 0.7-0.85 for highly expressed E. coli genes
highly_expressed_native.when: Reference set for E. coli codon usage
highly_expressed_native.why: Ribosomal proteins, elongation factors, and abundant outer membrane proteins define the reference set

low_expression_genes.when: Regulatory genes, transcription factors expressed at low levels
low_expression_genes.why: Low-expression genes do not face selection pressure for codon optimization

common_mistakes: Assuming CAI = 1.0 guarantees high expression (mRNA structure, RBS, promoter strength matter too)
Using CAI as sole metric — ignoring GC content, codon pair bias, and mRNA stability
Maximizing CAI by using the single most frequent codon for each amino acid (one amino acid-one codon approach) — this can deplete tRNA pools and reduce expression

optimization_strategy.description: Choosing between codon maximization, harmonization, and balanced optimization.

maximization.value_or_range: Select most frequent codon for each amino acid
maximization.when: Goal is maximum total protein yield; short genes; high-copy plasmid
maximization.why: Simple approach; maximizes CAI; works for many small proteins in E. coli

harmonization.value_or_range: Match codon frequency distribution to host (not just most frequent)
harmonization.when: Large or complex proteins requiring co-translational folding; multidomain proteins
harmonization.why: Preserves natural translation pauses that aid protein folding; rare codons at domain boundaries may be functionally important

multi_criteria.value_or_range: Simultaneously optimize CAI, GC content (40-60%), mRNA stability, and codon pair bias
multi_criteria.when: Production-grade optimization for therapeutic proteins or industrial enzymes
multi_criteria.why: No single metric captures all factors; mRNA structure at 5-prime end strongly affects translation initiation; host-specific requirements differ

when_NOT_to_optimize.value_or_range: Do not aggressively optimize if protein folding depends on translation rate modulation
when_NOT_to_optimize.when: Proteins with complex disulfide bonds, chaperone-dependent folding, or co-translational membrane insertion
when_NOT_to_optimize.why: Rare codons at domain boundaries slow translation, allowing co-translational folding; removing these pauses can cause aggregation

common_mistakes: Over-optimizing creates mRNA secondary structures that inhibit translation initiation
Ignoring the 5-prime end of the coding sequence (first 30-50 codons most critical for initiation)
Not checking for restriction sites, repeat sequences, or splice sites introduced by optimization
Using E. coli codon tables for expression in CHO cells or yeast

host_codon_tables.description: Sources for organism-specific codon usage frequency tables.

kazusa_database.when: Looking up codon usage for any organism
kazusa_database.why: Most comprehensive codon usage database; derived from GenBank CDS entries

CoCoPUTs.when: Need more current data than Kazusa (which was last updated 2007)
CoCoPUTs.why: CoCoPUTs provides updated tables based on current GenBank; Kazusa is based on older data

host_specific_considerations.value_or_range: E. coli: avoid AGG/AGA (Arg), CUA (Leu), AUA (Ile); CHO: balance GC content 45-55%; S. cerevisiae: prefer AT-rich codons
host_specific_considerations.when: Designing sequences for specific expression hosts
host_specific_considerations.why: Each host has different rare codons corresponding to low-abundance tRNAs; using these rare codons causes ribosome stalling

common_mistakes: Using the Kazusa table without checking the number of CDS entries for the organism (small sample = unreliable)
Not considering codon pair bias (adjacent codon context matters, not just individual codons)

codon_optimization.best_practice_notes: Use multi-criteria optimization tools (not just CAI maximization). Always minimize mRNA secondary structure at the 5-prime end (first 30-50 codons). Check for introduced restriction sites, cryptic splice sites, and Shine-Dalgarno-like sequences. Consider codon harmonization for complex proteins. Verify codon-optimized sequences with back-translation to confirm no unintended amino acid changes. Use host-specific rare codon supplementation (e.g., Rosetta strains for E. coli) when full optimization is not possible.

sbml_model_building.description: Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML) for encoding and sharing computational models of biological systems. Standards for model annotation, curation, and interoperability.

sbml_level_version.description: SBML specification version that determines available features and compatibility.

level_3_version_2.value_or_range: SBML Level 3 Version 2 (L3V2) — current recommended version
level_3_version_2.when: New model development; models requiring packages (FBC, comp, qual, multi)
level_3_version_2.why: Most current specification; supports modular packages for flux balance constraints (fbc), hierarchical composition (comp), qualitative models (qual); wider software support

level_2_version_5.when: Legacy models; compatibility with older tools; simple ODE/kinetic models
level_2_version_5.why: Most widely supported version historically; many BioModels entries are L2; some tools still lack full L3 support

fbc_package.value_or_range: L3 with FBC (Flux Balance Constraints) package v2
fbc_package.why: FBC package encodes gene-protein-reaction associations, flux bounds, and objective functions essential for FBA

common_mistakes: Using L2 when L3 packages are needed (e.g., for hierarchical model composition)
Not checking that target software supports the chosen SBML level/version
Converting between levels without validating that semantics are preserved

annotation_standards.description: MIRIAM-compliant annotation of model components with standardized identifiers.

miriam_compliance.value_or_range: All species, reactions, and compartments annotated with identifiers.org URIs
miriam_compliance.when: Any model intended for sharing, publication, or BioModels submission
miriam_compliance.why: MIRIAM (Minimum Information Required In the Annotation of Models) ensures reproducibility and interoperability; required for BioModels curation

sbo_terms.value_or_range: SBO (Systems Biology Ontology) terms on all reactions and species
sbo_terms.when: Model components need semantic typing (e.g., reaction is phosphorylation, species is protein)
sbo_terms.why: SBO provides controlled vocabulary; enables automated model analysis and comparison

rdf_annotation_format.value_or_range: RDF triples: (subject, qualifier, URI) using MIRIAM qualifiers (bqbiol:is, bqbiol:isVersionOf, etc.)
rdf_annotation_format.when: Linking model components to external databases (UniProt, ChEBI, GO, KEGG)
rdf_annotation_format.why: Standard format allows automated tools to extract and reason about model semantics

common_mistakes: No annotations at all — makes models unreproducible and unsearchable
Using free-text names instead of database identifiers
Incorrect MIRIAM qualifiers (e.g., using bqbiol:is when bqbiol:isVersionOf is appropriate)
Not validating SBML file with the SBML validator before sharing

sbml_model_building.best_practice_notes: Use SBML Level 3 for new models. Annotate everything with identifiers.org URIs. Validate models with the online SBML validator (sbml.org/validator). Use COPASI, libSBML, or python-libsbml for model creation. Submit curated models to BioModels database. Include units on all parameters. Use SBO terms for semantic typing. Test model behavior against published experimental data before sharing.

rna_secondary_structure_prediction.description: Computational prediction of RNA secondary structure using thermodynamic energy minimization (MFE), partition function methods, and comparative approaches.

energy_parameters.description: Nearest-neighbor thermodynamic parameters for RNA folding energy calculation.

turner_2004.value_or_range: Turner 2004 parameters (default in ViennaRNA, RNAfold, Mfold)
turner_2004.when: Standard RNA structure prediction at 37C, 1M NaCl
turner_2004.why: Most comprehensive and accurate parameter set from optical melting experiments; only modest improvement over Turner 1999; accuracy ~67% on benchmark sequences

turner_1999.when: Legacy predictions; comparing with older studies
turner_1999.why: Slightly less accurate than 2004 set but differences are small; accuracy limit is due to model assumptions, not parameter measurement errors

non_standard_temperature.value_or_range: Use ViennaRNA -T flag to set temperature; parameters extrapolated from 37C data
non_standard_temperature.when: Predicting structure at temperatures other than 37C (e.g., thermophilic organisms, in vitro at 25C)
non_standard_temperature.why: Free energy parameters have temperature dependence (deltaG = deltaH - T*deltaS); extrapolation valid within 20-50C range

common_mistakes: Not specifying which parameter set was used in publications
Assuming predictions are accurate at extreme temperatures (< 10C or > 60C)
Not accounting for ionic conditions — Turner parameters assume 1M NaCl; physiological conditions differ

prediction_accuracy.description: Expected accuracy of secondary structure prediction methods.

MFE_accuracy.value_or_range: ~65-70% sensitivity (base pairs correctly predicted) on benchmark datasets
MFE_accuracy.why: Simplified energy model (no pseudoknots, limited coaxial stacking) accounts for ~67% accuracy ceiling

partition_function_MEA.when: Maximum Expected Accuracy (MEA) structure from partition function base pair probabilities
partition_function_MEA.why: MEA considers ensemble of structures rather than single MFE; better at avoiding low-confidence base pairs

short_sequences.value_or_range: Higher accuracy for sequences < 200 nt; decreases for longer sequences
short_sequences.when: Predicting structure of small RNAs, aptamers, riboswitches
short_sequences.why: Shorter sequences have fewer alternative structures; energy model errors accumulate with length

long_sequences.value_or_range: Lower accuracy for > 500 nt; benchmark datasets typically limited to < 700 nt
long_sequences.why: Long-range base pairs poorly predicted; kinetic folding effects not captured by thermodynamic models; consider using LinearFold for better long-range predictions

common_mistakes: Treating MFE structure as the true structure — it is the single most stable structure, but the actual structure may differ
Not examining suboptimal structures or base pair probabilities
Assuming high negative MFE means the prediction is reliable (low energy does not equal high confidence)

pseudoknots.description: Crossing base pairs (pseudoknots) that cannot be predicted by standard dynamic programming algorithms.

standard_tools_no_pseudoknots.value_or_range: RNAfold, Mfold, RNAstructure do NOT predict pseudoknots
standard_tools_no_pseudoknots.why: Pseudoknot prediction is NP-hard for general case; standard DP algorithms exclude them

pseudoknot_capable.value_or_range: Use pKiss, HotKnots, IPknot, or DotKnot for pseudoknot prediction
pseudoknot_capable.when: Known or suspected pseudoknots (e.g., telomerase RNA, viral frameshifting elements)
pseudoknot_capable.why: These algorithms use specialized heuristics; accuracy still limited for complex pseudoknots

common_mistakes: Ignoring pseudoknots in functional RNAs where they are known to be essential (ribozymes, viral IRESes)
Using pseudoknot algorithms on very long sequences (exponential time complexity)

rna_secondary_structure_prediction.best_practice_notes: Always report which energy parameter set and software version were used. Examine base pair probabilities and the ensemble of structures, not just MFE. Use comparative sequence analysis (RNAalifold) when homologous sequences are available — significantly improves accuracy. For sequences > 500 nt, consider using LinearFold and window-based approaches. Validate computational predictions with experimental structure probing (SHAPE, DMS-seq) when possible.

biofilm_quantification_crystal_violet.description: Crystal violet (CV) staining assay for quantitative assessment of biofilm formation in microtiter plate format. Widely used for screening biofilm-forming capacity of bacterial isolates.

wavelength.description: Absorbance measurement wavelength for dissolved crystal violet dye.

OD570.when: Most common choice in published protocols; acetic acid or ethanol solubilization
OD570.why: Close to the absorbance maximum of crystal violet in 33% acetic acid (~585 nm); widely used in standard Stepanovic/O'Toole protocols

OD595.when: Alternative wavelength; some protocols and plate readers use this as default
OD595.why: Common in some published protocols; slightly off peak but still gives reliable relative quantification

optimal_wavelength.value_or_range: 580-585 nm (true absorbance maximum depends on solvent)
optimal_wavelength.why: Recent work (2025) shows optimal wavelength is 585 nm for 33% acetic acid and 580 nm for ethanol; using the true maximum improves reproducibility between labs

common_mistakes: Not being consistent with wavelength within a study — OD570 and OD595 give different absolute values
Not blanking against uninoculated stained wells (crystal violet can bind to plastic)
Using wavelengths far from absorbance maximum where signal-to-noise is poor

biofilm_classification.description: Cut-off values for categorizing biofilm-forming capacity.

stepanovic_classification.value_or_range: ODc = mean OD of negative control + 3*SD; Non-adherent: OD <= ODc; Weak: ODc < OD <= 2*ODc; Moderate: 2*ODc < OD <= 4*ODc; Strong: OD > 4*ODc
stepanovic_classification.why: Uses negative control (uninoculated medium) as baseline; accounts for inter-experiment variability

absolute_cutoffs.when: Quick classification without standardized negative controls
absolute_cutoffs.why: Absolute values depend on staining protocol, incubation time, and plate type; use relative (Stepanovic) method when possible

common_mistakes: Using absolute OD cut-offs without accounting for protocol-specific variation
Not including sufficient biological and technical replicates (minimum 3 biological x 3 technical)
Comparing OD values between different plate types (polystyrene vs polypropylene bind differently)

normalization.description: Whether and how to normalize biofilm OD to planktonic growth.

normalize_to_planktonic.when: Comparing strains with different growth rates; drug treatment experiments where growth is affected
normalize_to_planktonic.why: Accounts for differences in total biomass; slow-growing strains may appear as weak biofilm formers without normalization

no_normalization.when: All strains grow similarly; comparing same strain under different surface conditions
no_normalization.why: Normalization can introduce artifacts if planktonic OD is very low or variable

common_mistakes: Normalizing to planktonic growth when planktonic OD is near zero (division by small number)
Not reporting whether normalization was applied, making results incomparable between studies

biofilm_quantification_crystal_violet.best_practice_notes: Use polystyrene flat-bottom 96-well plates for consistency. Include minimum 3 biological replicates with 8 technical replicates each. Stain with 0.1% crystal violet for 15-20 min. Solubilize with 30% acetic acid or 95% ethanol. Read at 570 nm or 585 nm consistently. Always include uninoculated negative controls for classification. Report whether normalization to planktonic growth was applied. Follow the MBEC or Stepanovic protocol for reproducibility.

circular_dichroism_analysis.description: Circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy for estimating protein secondary structure content (alpha-helix, beta-sheet, turns, unordered) from far-UV spectra, using deconvolution algorithms.

wavelength_range.description: Spectral range needed for reliable secondary structure deconvolution.

far_UV_standard.why: Peptide bond n->pi* transition at ~220 nm and pi->pi* transition at ~190 nm carry secondary structure information; data below 190 nm improves deconvolution accuracy significantly

near_UV.when: Tertiary structure characterization; aromatic residue environment
near_UV.why: Trp (~290 nm), Tyr (~275 nm), Phe (~260 nm) side chains report on tertiary packing; useful for conformational change studies, not secondary structure

extended_far_UV.when: Maximum accuracy for secondary structure estimation; available at synchrotron facilities
extended_far_UV.why: VUV data below 190 nm significantly improves discrimination between beta-sheet and unordered structures

common_mistakes: Truncating spectra at 200 nm (missing critical information below 200 nm degrades deconvolution)
High absorption below 195 nm from buffer components (chloride ions, HEPES) — use phosphate buffer or Tris
Not purging instrument with nitrogen when measuring below 200 nm (O2 absorbs strongly)

protein_concentration_pathlength.description: Protein concentration and cuvette pathlength for optimal signal in far-UV CD.

far_UV_standard.value_or_range: 0.1-0.5 mg/mL protein in 1 mm pathlength cell
far_UV_standard.why: Gives absorbance of ~0.5-1.0 in the far-UV; good signal-to-noise; product of concentration x pathlength should give OD ~1.0 at 190 nm

far_UV_low_wavelength.when: Measuring down to 180 nm; minimizing buffer absorption
far_UV_low_wavelength.why: Shorter pathlength reduces buffer absorption; higher concentration maintains signal

near_UV.when: Near-UV CD (250-320 nm); aromatic residue analysis
near_UV.why: Near-UV signals are ~10x weaker than far-UV; need longer pathlength and/or higher concentration

common_mistakes: Protein concentration too high (OD > 2 at measurement wavelength — detector saturated)
Not knowing exact protein concentration — leads to wrong molar ellipticity conversion
Using quartz cuvettes with wrong pathlength tolerance

deconvolution_algorithm.description: Algorithm choice for estimating secondary structure fractions from CD spectra.

CDSSTR.value_or_range: CDSSTR algorithm — NRMSD ~0.007 for good fits
CDSSTR.when: Routine secondary structure estimation; DichroWeb server
CDSSTR.why: Generally gives lowest NRMSD values; uses variable selection from reference datasets; good for all-alpha and all-beta proteins

CONTINLL.value_or_range: CONTIN/LL algorithm — NRMSD ~0.03 for good fits
CONTINLL.when: Ridge regression approach; good with limited wavelength range
CONTINLL.why: More robust when data quality is suboptimal; regularized fitting prevents overfitting

SELCON3.value_or_range: SELCON3 algorithm — NRMSD ~0.07 for good fits
SELCON3.when: Self-consistent method; incorporates SVD with self-consistency check
SELCON3.why: Includes the query spectrum in the basis set; good for unusual proteins not well-represented in reference sets

best_practice.value_or_range: Run all three algorithms (CDSSTR, CONTINLL, SELCON3) and compare; consistent results increase confidence
best_practice.why: Different algorithms have different biases; concordance across methods is the best indicator of reliability

common_mistakes: Using only one algorithm without cross-validation
Not checking NRMSD — high values (>0.1) indicate poor fit or bad data
Using a reference set that does not include proteins similar to the query (e.g., all-alpha reference for a beta-barrel protein)

circular_dichroism_analysis.best_practice_notes: Measure far-UV CD from 190-260 nm minimum. Use phosphate or Tris buffer (avoid chloride, HEPES, PIPES below 200 nm). Determine protein concentration accurately (A280 with extinction coefficient, BCA assay, or amino acid analysis). Run three deconvolution algorithms and check consistency. Use DichroWeb (dichroweb.cryst.bbk.ac.uk) for online analysis. Report mean residue ellipticity [theta]_MRW in deg*cm^2/dmol. Include temperature and buffer conditions.

itc_binding_thermodynamics.description: Isothermal Titration Calorimetry (ITC) for measuring binding affinity (Ka), stoichiometry (n), enthalpy (deltaH), and entropy (deltaS) of molecular interactions in a single experiment.

c_value.description: Wiseman parameter c = n * Ka * [M], where n = stoichiometry, Ka = association constant, [M] = macromolecule concentration in the cell. Determines the shape of the titration isotherm.

optimal_range.when: Standard ITC experiment design for determining Ka, n, and deltaH simultaneously
optimal_range.why: c = 10-100 gives a sigmoidal isotherm with clear inflection point, allowing reliable determination of all three parameters

low_c_value.when: Weak binding (Kd > 10 uM); limited sample availability
low_c_value.why: Can still determine Kd and deltaH if stoichiometry is fixed (known from other methods) and ligand is in large excess; isotherm is shallow without clear inflection

high_c_value.why: Isotherm is too sharp (step function) — can determine n and deltaH but NOT Ka; need displacement (competition) ITC for Ka

common_mistakes: Not calculating c value before experiment — leads to wasted sample with uninterpretable data
Running high-c experiments and reporting Ka with false precision
Not fixing n when c < 5 (cannot independently determine both n and Ka from shallow isotherms)

injection_protocol.description: Number, volume, and spacing of injections of titrant into the cell.

standard_protocol.value_or_range: 15-25 injections; 1-3 uL each; 120-180 s spacing; first injection 0.4 uL (discarded)
standard_protocol.when: Standard binding experiment with ITC200 or PEAQ-ITC
standard_protocol.why: 15-25 points give sufficient data for reliable curve fitting; first injection is always discarded due to diffusion artifacts; spacing must allow return to baseline between injections

strong_signal.value_or_range: Up to 75 injections of 3 uL each (for high deltaH systems)
strong_signal.when: Binding produces large heat signal (|deltaH| > 10 kcal/mol)
strong_signal.why: More data points improve precision of Ka; can use smaller injection volumes when signal is strong

weak_signal.why: Larger volumes produce more measurable heat per injection; fewer injections avoid excessive dilution

common_mistakes: Not discarding first injection — always contains systematic error
Injection spacing too short — baseline not recovered between injections
Not reaching saturation — need to continue injections past the equivalence point to define the baseline

concentration_ratio.description: Ratio of ligand (syringe) to macromolecule (cell) concentration.

standard_1_to_1.why: Ensures titration goes from undersaturation to well beyond saturation; allows accurate determination of stoichiometry and baseline

cell_concentration.value_or_range: [M] in cell = 10-50 uM (typical for protein-ligand); > 5 uM minimum
cell_concentration.when: Standard ITC for moderate affinity (Kd = 10 nM - 100 uM)
cell_concentration.why: Must produce detectable heat (> 0.1 ucal/injection); lower [M] needs higher deltaH or lower cell volume

common_mistakes: Buffer mismatch between syringe and cell solutions — causes large heats of dilution that obscure binding
Not performing blank titrations (ligand into buffer, buffer into macromolecule) for subtraction
Concentrations determined inaccurately — stoichiometry n will be wrong if [M] is wrong

binding_model_selection.description: Choosing the appropriate thermodynamic model for fitting ITC data.

one_site_model.value_or_range: Independent identical binding sites model (most common)
one_site_model.when: Expected simple 1:1 binding; n is a fitted parameter near 1.0
one_site_model.why: Simplest model; fits n, Ka, and deltaH; n deviating from expected integer may indicate inactive protein

two_site_model.value_or_range: Two sets of independent sites with different affinities
two_site_model.when: Clear biphasic isotherm with two transitions; proteins with two distinct binding sites
two_site_model.why: Requires sufficient data quality to resolve two Ka and two deltaH values; need clear separation of affinities (>10-fold different)

sequential_model.when: Cooperative binding where each site has different affinity depending on occupancy of other sites
sequential_model.why: Accounts for cooperativity; more parameters require higher quality data

common_mistakes: Using a two-site model when data quality only supports one-site (overfitting)
Fixing stoichiometry n to an assumed value without justification
Not considering that apparent n < 1 often means some protein is inactive, not fractional binding
Ignoring heats of dilution in the fitting

itc_binding_thermodynamics.best_practice_notes: Calculate c value before running experiments to ensure interpretable results (c = 10-100 ideal). Dialyze or gel-filtrate both macromolecule and ligand into identical buffer to minimize heats of dilution. Always run blank titrations (ligand-into-buffer and buffer-into-macromolecule). Discard the first injection point. Determine protein concentration accurately (A280 preferred over BCA for ITC). Start with the simplest binding model (one-site) and only add complexity if statistically justified. Report deltaG, deltaH, -TdeltaS, and n with errors.
